parts: Did you turn the banknote over? There is a bridge on the back.
Every euro note has one, and every note has a different bridge.
Here is the strange part. The bank says the bridges are not real ones.
Yet one bridge magazine editor, according to a podcast, thought he recognized some of them.
So why are the bridges on euro banknotes not real?
Look at the front of a note first. There are windows and doorways.
The European Central Bank says they stand for openness and cooperation in Europe.
On the back, the bridges. The bank says they stand for communication, between the people of Europe, and between Europe and the rest of the world.
On the lower notes, each has its own architectural style. Classical on the five, Romanesque on the ten, Gothic on the twenty, Renaissance on the fifty, baroque on the hundred.
So the bridges give you a tour of European history. But the bank says none of those windows, doorways, or bridges is an actual existing monument.
Why not use real ones? Think about designing money for many countries at once.
Every country would want its own famous bridge on the note.
According to the podcast Ninety-Nine Percent Invisible, the contest rules barred national heroes, national symbols, and national monuments.
In nineteen ninety-six, a design by Robert Kalina, of the Austrian national bank, won. The winner was announced in December.
So the logic seems simple. If every bridge is invented, no country wins and no country loses.
But here is the twist. Wikipedia says the early designs showed real bridges, including the Rialto in Venice.
They were redrawn to look more generic.
The podcast adds a story. A bridge magazine editor, Russ Swan, looked at the finished notes, and thought he recognized real bridges behind them.
One looked like a bridge in northern France, which he had visited just weeks before.
Kalina says in the podcast: I thought the bridges were generic enough, but apparently not.
That story comes from one podcast, so take the details with a pinch of salt. The bank's own position is clear: the bridges are not real.
Now the best part. Someone decided to make them real.
A Dutch artist, Robin Stam, designed seven bridges in Spijkenisse, a town near Rotterdam. Each one is based on one of the seven bridges on the banknotes.
They are built in colored concrete, around a housing estate.
People can cross them on foot or by bike. Euronews says they are within walking distance of each other.
The sources disagree on when. Some say two thousand eleven. Others say two thousand thirteen.
So the invented bridges became real bridges. The money came first. The concrete came later.
The newer Europa banknotes kept the same idea: windows and doorways on the front, bridges on the back.
The bank says the portrait of Europa in them comes from a vase in the Louvre.
Now the bank is choosing a design for a future series. Two themes are on the shortlist: European culture, and rivers and birds.
It expects to decide around the end of two thousand twenty-six. After that, it will take several years before new notes reach your pocket, and your current notes keep their value.
Next time you hold a banknote, play a game. Check the number and guess the period.
Gothic on the twenty. Renaissance on the fifty. Then find the bridge on the back, and try to find its twin in real life.
You will probably not find an exact match. That is the idea.
So a euro banknote is a careful fiction. It holds a tour of European history, with no official address.
Now put it back in your wallet, and walk into a supermarket. Grab a shopping cart.
Why did shoppers once need convincing to use one?
